summary: MISSION CONTROL is a browser game for the "Space Mission Design Game" challenge. The player is the flight director: you get a science goal, a budget and engineering limits, then build a spacecraft in 3D, choose an orbit and a rocket, fly the launch, and run the mission day by day, answering real-world problems such as radiation upsets or a failing reaction wheel. Everything is calculated with real equations (rocket equation, orbits, radio links, eclipses, radiation, heat, Mars launch windows), and a final debrief shows what went wrong and what would have scored higher. It includes 5 missions, 79 parts, 13 test campaigns, a technology tree where every node names a real-world analogue, a delta-v map and a real-data page comparing the game with real rockets and missions. It runs in any browser with no install. The goal is to let students feel how mass, power, orbit, cost and schedule trade off in real mission design.
details:
What it does: You design a spacecraft from 79 parts in a 3D workshop (mass, power, cost and delta-v update live), pick instruments and an orbit, choose a launch vehicle (interplanetary targets also need a launch date inside a planetary window), book verification tests, fly the ascent and injection burn, then operate the mission for months. 16 types of anomaly can strike; your responses affect the score. A debrief explains the result and re-simulates alternative decisions.

How it works: A deterministic simulation engine in TypeScript implements the rocket equation, vis-viva and Hohmann transfers, link budgets, eclipse length from the beta angle, atmospheric drag, radiation dose, a thermal balance and launch windows. A technology tree (31 nodes), a delta-v map and a "Real data" page compare the game with real launchers and missions.

Impact: It makes mission design learnable by anyone, in a browser, with no install. There are four visual themes, adjustable text size, keyboard shortcuts and a phone-friendly layout.

Tools: TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js (3D), Vitest (86 automated tests), GitHub Pages. Everything is generated by code: no photos, no downloaded assets.

Creativity: Real physics wrapped in a playable build-fly-learn loop, with a debrief that teaches why a mission succeeded or failed.

Honest limits: part specifications and scores are illustrative game values; real reference figures are rounded. Team mode syncs tabs of one browser only. Sound was not user-tested.
dataRefs: NASA Planetary Fact Sheets (Earth, Moon, Mars)
